newsitem.title: FRANCE: Asia/Pacific to lead $1 trillion electronics market.
newsitem.headline: Asia/Pacific to lead $1 trillion electronics market.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
World electronics production will easily breach $1.2 trillion by the year 2000, and will be led by companies from the new Asian economies, according to a U.S. high technology consultancy.

Production of personal computers, the semiconductor industry 00and communications and multimedia devices will be worth $1,200 billion in 2000, compared with $750 billion last year, and will reach $2,200 billion by 2010, Dataquest analyst Jim Eastlake told a conference here on Tuesday.
Asia/Pacific companies from countries other than Japan, like South Korea and Singapore, will edge ahead of north America in 1999 to account for just over 30 per cent of the world's market by 2000.
North America's share will dip to just under 30 per cent, with Europe and Japan each with slightly over 20 per cent, Dataquest said.
This charge will be led by the personal computer.
"The PC contains almost half of all the chips and electronic hardware produced," Eastlake told a symposium organised by Dataquest's owners, Gartner Group.

"Our research shows a continuing explosion in worldwide personal computer sales. This year sales will jump 20 per cent to just over 70 million (PCs), and we expect each of the next three years to grow around 18 per cent to hit just under 120 million in 1999," Eastlake said.
Although powerful growth by most industry standards, this represents a slight slowing from 1994's 23 per cent and 1995's 24 percent.
"We also expect to see wireless communications show torrid growth," Eastlake said.

Everybody can see the ubiquity of personal computers. But the computer chip invasion has crept into almost all facets of life, driven by the hidden use of semiconductors, or computer chips, which provide the brains and power behind their use in the form of microprocessors, memory, transistors, and logic circuits.
Chips now manage automobile engines and their new safety systems like air bags and anti-lock brakes. They manage electronic wrist-watches, mobile phones, and there is much more to come.
In the next few years chips will appear in multimedia devices for video-conferencing, interactive television, and "set-top box" devices to transform TVs into personal computers.

New medical electronic devices like body scanning and monitoring equipment, electronic metering of domestic gas and electric supplies, while even mundane devices like the humble domestic light bulb will be made more efficient thanks to the chip.

According to Dataquest, Intel Corp of the U.S. is still the number one producer of semiconductors, closely followed by the Japanese firms NEC, Toshiba, and Hitachi. But at number six and 10 respectively are South Korean relative newcomers Samsung Electronics Co and Hyundai Group. LG Semicon is another contender from South Korea.
Eastlake makes the point that no European company appears in the top 10, although Philips Electronics of the Netherlands is eleventh.

Dataquest forecast that semiconductor business alone will reach $310 billion by 2000 and $700 billion by 2005. In 1995 and 1996 the figure was stuck at around $150 billion, because of a slowing of U.S. business investment, and over-optimistic expections for Microsoft Corp's new Windows 95 software.

And as production increases, so will their power and sophistication rise and costs drop -- good news for the computerphobic who can look forward to personal computers becoming simpler and more user-friendly.
